title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet V: the killing of Humbaba
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), SB V) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet V: 121 of 274 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
The heroes enter the Forest of Cedar, confront Humbaba, and with the help of Shamash's winds overpower him. Humbaba pleads for his life and curses them; they kill him, fell the cedars, and float a great cedar door down the Euphrates to Nippur.

The Standard Babylonian version of the epic, traditionally ascribed to the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni, was written on twelve tablets. Most surviving copies come from the libraries of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE) and from Babylon and other Babylonian cities (7th-2nd century BCE). This page gives Tablet V in the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition by A. R. George (2022 and later revisions).

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/V) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 121 of the 274 lines of the eBL edition (44%), from 5 tablets in the British Museum: K.3252 (Nineveh), K.8591 (Nineveh), K.13525 (Nineveh), Sm.866 (Nineveh), Sm.209 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 153 of the 274 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 20-27 (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 85-90 (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 115-135 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 143-151 (no manuscript preserves it); 152-183 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 184-187 (no manuscript preserves it); 190-194 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 199 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 202-204 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 207 (no manuscript preserves it); 247-252 (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 253-267 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 268 (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 269-270 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 271-272 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 273 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 274-276 (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 284-285 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 286 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 287-298 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 299-309a (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 309b (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum)); 310-317 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447); 323 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76985 (Iraq Museum); not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): T.1447). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; * collated sign; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; / alternative readings; : divider sign written on the tablet.

translation.text:
1They stood marvelling at the forest,
2gazing at the lofty cedars,
3gazing at the forest’s entrance –
4Where Ḫumbaba came and went there was a track,
5the paths were in good order and the way was well trodden.
6They were gazing at the Cedar Mountain,
7the dwelling of the gods, the throne-dais of the goddesses,
8[on the] very face of the mountain the cedar was proffering its abundance,
9sweet was its shade, full of delight.
10[Thick] tangled was the thorn, the forest a shrouding canopy,
11cedars and gum trees, [all entwined,] left no way in.
12For a league on all sides cedars [lifts up] saplings,
13cypresses [grew thick] for two-thirds of a league.
14Cedars scabbed with resin grew sixty cubits high,
15the resin [oozed] forth, drizzling down like rain,
16[flowing freely] for ravines to bear away.
17[Through] all the forest a bird began to sing,
18[hen birds] gave answer, a constant din was the noise.
19[A solitary] tree-cricket set off a noisy chorus,

translation.text:
28[terror] fell on Gilgameš.
29[Stiffness took] a grip on his arms,
30and tremors beset his legs.
31[Enkidu] opened his mouth to speak, saying to Gilgameš:
32‘[Let us go deep] into the midst of the forest,
33[let us get] going and raise a loud cry!’
34[Gilgameš] opened his mouth to speak, saying to Enkidu:
35‘[Why,] my friend, do we tremble like cowards,
36[we who] came across all the mountains?
37‘[Shall] … before us?
38Before we have withdrawn…
39‘My [friend] is one who is tested in combat,
40one who has been in battle has no fear of death.
41‘You have been splashed in blood, so you need not fear death:
42[go] berserk, like a dervish fall into a frenzy.
43Let [your shout] boom loud [like] a kettle drum,
44may stiffness leave your arms, the tremors depart from your legs!’
45‘Take my hand, friend, and we shall go [on] together,
46[let] your thoughts dwell on combat!
47Forget death and [seek] life!
48[The one who] walks alongside is the prudent man.
49‘“[Let him who] goes first be on guard for himself and bring his comrade to safety!”
50It is they made a name [for days] long in the future!’
51[At the] distant … they both arrived,
52[they ceased] their talking and came to a halt.
53They stood marvelling at the forest,
54[…]
